items.text: All provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898

segments.text: The CrPC provides the procedural machinery for criminal cases—from information and investigation to inquiry, trial, judgment, sentence and post-trial remedies.

Study it as a criminal-case timeline: complaint/FIR → arrest and investigation → remand/bail → cognizance → charge → trial → evidence → judgment/sentence → appeal/revision. Also understand powers of police, magistrates and courts.
Primary authority: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, as currently amended.

blocks.text: Criminal procedure as a liberty-sensitive process

segments.text: The CrPC provides the procedural route through which allegations become investigated cases and, where legally justified, prosecutions and trials. Because the process authorizes coercive powers such as arrest, search, remand and compulsory attendance, procedure is not mere administration. It is a framework for both enforcement and safeguards.

The easiest learning method is chronological: information or complaint; investigation; arrest where lawful; production before the competent judicial authority; remand or bail questions; police report or complaint proceedings; cognizance; charge; trial; evidence; judgment and sentence; and appeal, revision or other post-trial remedies.

Police investigate and collect material within their legal powers. Prosecutors represent the public case in the manner prescribed by law. Magistrates and trial courts exercise judicial powers such as remand, bail, cognizance, framing of charge and adjudication according to jurisdiction. Higher courts exercise appellate, revisional, constitutional or other supervisory powers where law permits.

These functions should not be blurred. Investigation is not a judicial finding of guilt, and an accusation in an FIR is not itself proof. The trial is the process in which admissible evidence is tested and legal responsibility is determined by the competent court.

Bail concerns release from custody on legally defined terms while proceedings continue; it is not an acquittal. Remand concerns lawful judicial authorization for continued custody within the limits and purposes recognized by procedure. Both issues directly engage personal liberty and therefore require a legal basis rather than routine administrative treatment.

Cognizance is the court’s formal taking up of an offence for judicial proceedings under the procedural framework. Charge identifies the accusation to be tried. Confusing the two leads to a distorted case timeline.

A procedural problem should be answered by locating the case at the correct stage. Ask what has already happened, which authority presently has power, what legal safeguard applies, and what the next lawful step is. This stage-based method is more reliable than recalling isolated sections without context.

items.text: The CrPC is the procedural route through which criminal law is enforced. The PPC may define an offence, but the CrPC explains how the case moves from information and investigation to trial and post-trial remedies.
Learn the stages as a timeline:

information or complaint; investigation; arrest where lawful; remand or bail questions; submission of material to court; cognizance; charge; trial and evidence; judgment and sentence; appeal or revision.

Different institutions perform different functions. Police investigate, prosecutors conduct the prosecution, magistrates and courts exercise judicial powers, and higher courts perform appellate or supervisory functions within law.
Bail and remand should be studied as liberty-related decisions, not as routine paperwork. A good answer links legal authority, necessity, judicial oversight and procedural safeguards.
Cognizance and charge are not the same. Cognizance concerns the court taking judicial notice of an offence for proceedings; charge identifies the accusation that will be tried.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not merge investigation and trial. Investigation collects and tests material; trial is the judicial process in which criminal responsibility is determined.

items.text: Create one flowchart for a police-report case and one for a complaint case.
Prepare arrest, remand, bail, cognizance, charge, trial and appeal as separate modules.
Understand the roles of police, magistrate, prosecutor and trial court.
Use current bare-act wording for exact powers and timelines.

segments.text: Keep the sequence of proceedings clear; procedural confusion is a major source of weak answers.
CrPC is procedural; PPC is substantive.
Investigation collects material; trial judicially determines guilt.
Bail, remand and arrest affect liberty and therefore require legal authority.
Cognizance and charge are different stages.
Appeal and revision are distinct corrective mechanisms.
